## Methods

Preparing Ontology Datasets for Model Training

Representative Protein Sequences: The UniRef90 and UniRef50 datasets were collected from the UniProt database29. The UniRef90 dataset containing 166 million representative protein sequences was created by clustering UniRef100 sequences that are 11 or more residues long, ensuring that each cluster contains sequences with at least 90% identity and 80% overlap with the longest sequence in the cluster. The UniRef100 sequences consolidate identical sequences and sub-fragments of 11 or more residues from any organism into a single entry, displaying a representative protein sequence along with the accession numbers of all merged entries and links to the corresponding UniProtKB and UniParc records. UniRef50 containing 59 million representative protein sequences is formed by clustering UniRef90 seed sequences that share at least 50% sequence identity and 80% overlap with the longest sequence in the cluster. We further annotated these datasets and used them for model training.

Protein Species and Function Annotation: The UniProtKB dataset was downloaded from the UniProt database29. UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB) is a comprehensive repository of functional information on proteins, encompassing amino acid sequences, protein names or descriptions, taxonomic data, widely accepted biological ontologies, classifications, cross-references, and clear indications of annotation quality, including evidence attribution for both experimental and computational data. The UniProtKB dataset includes functional information for approximately 250 million proteins. For our purposes, we extracted taxonomic information, cellular component data, molecular function details, and biological process information from the UniProtKB dataset to annotate the representative protein sequences in the UniRef90 and UniRef50 datasets. The taxonomic lineage information was preserved from the superkingdom level down to the species level. Overall, 107,891 unique taxonomic terms were retained in the annotated UniRef90 and UniRef50 datasets. The functional annotation of proteins includes Gene Ontology (GO) terms and Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers. The annotated UniRef90 and UniRef50 datasets contain 30,391 unique GO function terms and 9,217 EC function terms.

Protein Structure Annotation: The protein structures were collected from PDB52, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database53, and ESM Metagenomic Atlas30. The PDB is an archive of experimentally determined 3D structural data for large biological molecules, such as proteins, DNA, and RNA, which is crucial for research and education in fundamental biology, health, energy, and biotechnology. AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and ESM Metagenomic Atlas archive of protein structure predicted by AlphaFold3 and ESMfold30, respectively. For annotating the UniRef90 and UniRef50 datasets, we used experimentally validated protein structures and high-quality predicted protein structures with pTM > 0.7 and pLDDT > 0.7. These protein structures were then classified into SCOPe Class, Fold, and Superfamily classification for further annotation. The Structural Classification of Proteins—extended (SCOPe) is a database that builds upon the SCOPe database, which is a manually curated hierarchy of domains from most proteins with known structures, organized according to structural and evolutionary relationships. The classification includes Classes based primarily on secondary structure content and organization, Folds grouping structurally similar superfamilies, and Superfamilies that connect protein families with common functional and structural features inferred from a common evolutionary ancestor.

Protein Characteristics Annotation: The protein characteristics data were collected from literature, including the thermal stability of 48,000 proteins across 13 species ranging from archaea to humans and covering melting temperatures of 30–90 °C27, 8926 proteins of high thermal stability from Archaea species living in an extreme high-temperature environment54, 58 689 soluble and 70 954 insoluble proteins28, 25693 signal peptides that control protein secretion and translocation in all living organisms55, and protein subcellular localizations collected from SwissProt56 and Human protein atlas57. These data were used to train USM models in the quality control pipeline.

Tokenizer Construction

We constructed a byte-pair encoding (BPE)58 tokenizer tailored for protein design, with a vocabulary size of 49,152. To support flexibility in encoding heterogeneous biological inputs, we reserved 200 token IDs as special tokens, which can be dynamically replaced at runtime to represent ontology terms, annotations, or experimental constraints. The reserved token set is drawn from a comprehensive replacement resource pool encompassing digits, Latin and Greek alphabets, punctuation (! " # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . / : ; < = > ? @ [ \ ] ^ _ ` { | } ~), whitespace characters (space \t \n \r \x0b \x0c), custom tokens (<CLS>, <PAD>, <MASK>, <EOD>, <:>), and additional domain-specific symbols (£, ¥, «, », ±, ·). This design ensures broad coverage for encoding biological prompt phrases and precise parsing of specialized terminology, such as protein functional annotations and enzyme classification numbers (e.g., EC:1.1.1.181).

During tokenization, each protein sequence was segmented into BPE subword tokens, optimized to capture both short functional motifs (e.g., catalytic triads, signal peptides) and long repetitive patterns (e.g., coiled-coils, tandem repeats). Ontology inputs—including functional annotations, EC numbers, structural constraints, and protein family names—were tokenized separately using the special token pool and subsequently concatenated with the protein tokens to form unified input sequences. In total, this process produced over 60 billion tokens from the integrated protein sequence and annotation datasets, which were used to train the PGM model.

The Protein Design Agent (PDA)

The Protein Design Agent (PDA) serves as the orchestration layer that translates user requirements into ontology prompts and function calls to the Protein Generation Model (PGM). In our protein design agent (PDA), we use a module similar to Gorilla22 and Toolformer23, to convert users’ task requirements to function calls of our models.

Supervised Fine-tuning with LoRA: To achieve this goal, we perform low-rank parameter adaption (LoRA) 59 on the open-sourced large language model Gemma2-2B60. The model is fine-tuned for 1 epoch with a single pass of all data. The batch size is 32 and the learning rate is 1e-4. The rank for LoRA is 16.

To obtain the training data, we use GPT4 to generate input and output pairs for each function and characteristic by providing GPT4 with the input requirements and functionality description of each function and characteristic. The inputs are the user’s requirements and the outputs are the corresponding function and characteristic ontology prompts and model function calls. We also provide high-quality examples generated by human experts as examples to GPT4 for the generation. Finally, we collected 5000 pairs of data generated by GPT4 and used GPT4 to score these generated data based on the scope of requirements and the correctness of ontology prompts and function calls. We further validated the correctness of the data with human experts. We used the top 2000 scoring data pairs for training. In addition, to detect unsupported requirements, we extracted 200 input prompts from the Stanford Alpaca dataset and designated the corresponding outputs as “unsupported”.

The Protein Generation Model (PGM)

To train the protein generation model (PGM), we adopt a prompt-based encoding schema. The sequence begins with ontology tokens that provide conditioning context, introduced at the first position of the sequence. The ontology context typically contains 5–30 tokens, depending on the granularity of the annotation (e.g., “enzyme class EC:1.1.1.181” or “IgG1 antibody heavy chain”). In contrast, protein sequences are substantially longer, ranging from 100 to 1000 tokens after BPE segmentation. The input structure follows the format:
<CLS> Ontology_Tokens <:> Protein_Tokens <EOD>
This design ensures that ontology context acts as a prefix, guiding generation while preserving autoregressive protein modeling. All tokens (protein and ontology) are mapped into a shared embedding space via a learnable embedding layer. Positional encodings are applied to preserve order. Ontology tokens, although distinct in semantics, share the embedding matrix with protein tokens to enable the transfer of contextual information. This joint representation allows the PGM model to attend simultaneously to biological prompts and sequence context during self-attention, enabling it to learn the statistical patterns and relationships among protein sequences, structures and biological functions.

PGM is an autoregressive large language model that shares similarities with the decoder-only architecture used in LLaMA serial models. PGM consists of embedding layers, multiple decoder blocks, and multilayer perceptron (MLP) layers. The embedding layer maps each token to a continuous vector representation, capturing its unique properties. The decoder blocks capture the sequential dependencies between tokens, allowing the model to learn the context and relationships between functions and protein sequences. The decoder block follows the standard transformer architecture62, applies RMSNorm for pre-normalization 63 and multi-head attentions, uses the SwiGLU activation function 64, and rotary positional embeddings 65. The MLP layers consist of a fully connected layer and a normalization layer, which are responsible for generating the final output tokens that represent the generated protein sequences. The 3B PGM model consists of 24 decoder blocks and 24 multi-head attentions, with embedding dimensions of 3072. For evaluation purposes, we also trained PGM models with parameter sizes of 1 billion (1B), 3 billion (3B), and 7 billion (7B). The annotated UniRef90 dataset and UniRef50 were utilized to train these models, respectively. After evaluation, we used the 3B PGM model as the default protein generation model in ORI.

The model is trained under a causal language modeling (CLM) objective, predicting the next token given the concatenated prefix–protein sequence. Formally, given ontology tokens O = (o , ... ,o ) and protein tokens P = (p ,...,p ), the training objective is:

The Unified Sequence Model (USM)

We proposed unified sequence model (USM) models to make fast and accurate predictions of protein characteristics. The architecture of the USM is similar to the conventional Encoder Only Transformer model, as shown in Supplementary Figure 1. The model takes a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) Token MT ∈ NM×L as input, where N represents the set of non-negative integers, M is the number of sequences (I1 for single sequence input), and L is the sequence length. The output is denoted as O ∈ RB×L×D, where R represents the set of real numbers, B is the batch size, and D is the dimension of the embedding. The first layer of the model is the MSA Embedding layer, which embeds the discrete MSA Tokens. The core of the USM model consists of multiple USM Transformer Blocks, which extract features from the MSA. The final output is generated by the language model (LM) head layer. The LM Head layer consists of RMSNorm and Linear layers, which transform the MSA features into language probability outputs. Compared to the MSA Transformer model66, the USM Transformer Block design is illustrated in Supplementary Figure 1. It consists of three parts: Column Attention, Fast Row Attention, and SwiGLU Activation. Assuming the MSA features h ∈ RB × row × col × D, where row represents the number of rows in the MSA and col represents the number of columns. The Row Attention is similar to the conventional Multihead Attention and has a computational complexity of O(hdLM2). The Column Attention can be simplified as a transposed form of Row Attention, with a computational complexity of O(hdML2), where h is the number of attention heads, d is the head dimension, M is the number of sequences in the MSA, and L is the sequence length.

Unlike the MSA Transformer Block, the USM Block starts with Column Attention. The USM Block consists of three major parts: Column Attention, Fast Row Attention, and SwiGLU Activation. The Column Attention consists of Transpose and Multi-head Attention layers. We proposed a method called Fast Row Attention (FRA) based on the assumption of redundancy along the Column direction in MSA data, which leads to sparsity in the MSA features h along the same direction. To achieve this, we apply Average Pooling along the Column direction, reducing the MSA features h to h_row ∈ RB×row. This operation speeds up the subsequent Multi-Attention by a factor of col, and the computational complexity of Fast Row Attention is O(hdL2). By leveraging Fast Row Attention, the USM model demonstrates significantly improved speed and the ability to handle larger parameter sizes. SwiGLU Activation is a type of MLP layer that consists of Linear and SiLU activation functions. Additionally, we enhance the model's ability to extrapolate long sequences by combining Multihead Attention with Rotary Position Embedding (ROPE).

When there is only one sequence in the MSA input, the USM can be considered as a single sequence (SS) model and the Column Attention degenerates into an MLP. When degenerating into a single sequence model, the USM is similar to the ESM model, highlighting its versatility. The USM model can be used as both an MSA model and an SS model.

The USM model is trained using the Masked Token prediction approach, similar to the conventional BERT model training 67. The existing Masked Token method typically uses a fixed masking ratio, such as 0.15, during model training. However, due to the large number of MSA sequences, the tokens along the Column direction are often similar. This results in lower training efficiency with smaller masking ratios. To address this, we propose a dynamic Mask Token method that combines two masking schemes:
Column Random Masking: This operation randomly masks entire columns. Since learning from column masking is more challenging, we use a smaller proportion, set to 5% in our approach.
Global Random Masking: This operation applies dynamic masking with varying proportions. It randomly masks individual tokens. The masking ratio decreases gradually during training, starting from 0.3 and decreasing to 0.15.

The objective function for training the USM model is defined as follows:

Iterative Optimization with Wet Lab Feedback

Wet lab experiments are crucial in developing protein generative models as they provide valuable biological insights into the functionalities of the generated proteins. These insights are essential for validating the accuracy and effectiveness of the models. However, it is often observed that only a subset of these proteins exhibit the desired functionalities and activities, while the majority do not show significant activity. To improve the performance of these models, researchers often analyze the outcomes of wet lab experiments and devise heuristic methods to refine or retrain the models. However, this approach heavily relies on the subjective expertise of individual researchers, which can introduce variability and limit reproducibility.

To address this challenge, we propose a framework that is named Reinforcement Learning from Wet-lab Feedback (RLWF). This framework utilizes feedback from wet lab experiments and selectively incorporates generated data to optimize model preference. Doing so systematically increases the likelihood of generating protein sequences with the targeted properties.

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has been effectively employed to optimize the output of Large Language Models (LLMs), aligning the generated responses with user preferences68. In this approach, a dataset D containing preference pairs (x, yw, yl)—comprising a prompt x, a preferred response yw, and a less preferred response yl—is utilized. The model π is then optimized to favor yw over yl. An alternative to RLHF, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)69, simplifies this by minimizing the loss of DPO, using a fixed reference model π : ref

Iterative enhancements of RLHF, such as Iterative DPO 35,36,70, have been developed to iteratively refine the model. This method involves generating a set of new preference pairs using the current model, evaluating them via a reward model or human judgment, and optimizing the model on this preference dataset using DPO in each iteration.

Our framework adopts this iterative approach to refine the model for a given prompt x, for example, “<Glucosaminidase><temperature90><:>”. In the first iteration, both the reference model and the current model are initialized with the pre-trained model.The reference model is fixed.

At the start of each iteration, the current model is used to generate protein sequences by repeatedly feeding it the prompt x. This process is repeated 10,000 times to obtain a dataset, S₀, comprising 10,000 sequences. Virtual screening is then performed to identify a subset of promising candidates, S₁ (typically ~100 sequences), for wet-lab validation. The remaining 9,900 sequences form the set S₂.

For the sequences in S₂, we estimate their perplexity using the reference model and select the top K sequences with the highest perplexity to form the set 𝑆 . We also evaluate their predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) scores and select the K sequences with the lowest scores to form the set 𝑆 . The intersection of 𝑆 and 𝑆 is used as the set of unpreferred responses, Sl. The value of K is chosen such that the size of Sl is greater than 100; in practice, K is set to 500. The preferred responses set, Sw, is defined as S₁.

We then construct the training dataset D using all possible pairs of preferred (yw ∈ Sw) and unpreferred (yl ∈ Sl) responses. This selection is based on the premise that the model should generate more functionally expressive sequences, while avoiding those preferred by the current model yet less likely to exhibit desired functionality.

The model is fine-tuned using the R-DPO loss for one epoch over the dataset D. The updated model is subsequently used as the current model in the next iteration, which is used to generate new sequences for testing, following the same process to construct the preference dataset and optimize the model. The reference model in each iteration is a fixed copy of the model updated in the previous iteration. The model loss of the generated sequences is estimated by the auto-regressive loss of the reference model.

Benchmark with Baseline Methods

To comprehensively evaluate ORI, we benchmarked it against a wide range of recent state-of-the-art models, spanning conditioned protein generation and thermostability optimization.

ProteinSGM: ProteinSGM is a score-based diffusion model that produces native-like protein structures11. We used the crystal structure of hen egg-white lysozyme (PDB ID: 132L) and T4 lysozyme (PDB ID: 216L) as a template, where specific regions were masked to provide partial structural information as input. ProteinSGM was then used to generate 1000 conditional 6D coordinates from the ProteinSGM model, including Cβ–Cβ distances, ω and θ dihedral angles, and ϕ planar angles. These coarse-grained 6D representations were then converted into full-atom protein backbones using Rosetta MinMover42, which performed constrained backbone minimization to ensure physically realistic geometries.

ProGen3: ProGen3 is an autoregressive protein language model designed for sequence generation12. We provided the sequences of hen egg-white lysozyme (PDB ID: 132L) and T4 lysozyme (PDB ID: 216L) as conditioning contexts. Using these templates, we employed the ProGen3-3B model to generate amino acid sequences in both N-to-C (forward) and C-to-N (reverse) directions, conditioned on the functional and sequence constraints. A total of 1000 protein sequences were sampled, ensuring coverage of diverse sequence space.

Evo2: Evo 2 is a large-scale biological foundation model trained on 9.3 trillion DNA bases that learns genome-wide biological features directly from DNA sequence, enabling accurate prediction of functional variants and controllable genome-scale sequence generation37. For Evo2-based conditional protein generation, we first designed functional prompts according to the model’s requirements, encoding structural and biochemical features of target proteins. Specifically, we constructed text-based prompts describing hen egg-white lysozyme (PDB ID: 132L) and T4 lysozyme (PDB ID: 216L), including their structural class, enzymatic activity, and functional attributes. Conditioned on these prompts, Evo2 was used to generate 1,000 DNA sequences for each protein, ensuring that the outputs satisfied the specified biochemical and functional constraints. The generated DNA sequences were subsequently translated into protein sequences, followed by filtering to remove incomplete or invalid coding regions before downstream evaluation.

ProteinMPNN: ProteinMPNN is a graph-based generative model for protein sequence design conditioned on backbone structures39. For thermostability optimization, we first predicted the backbone structure of each target protein using AlphaFold23, which served as the input scaffold. ProteinMPNN was then applied to redesign the amino acid sequences on this backbone. For each target, we generated 1000 redesigned variants and selected the top 100 candidates based on the predicted stability score. The redesigned sequences were further filtered by predicted folding quality (pLDDT > 70) to ensure structural plausibility.

Rosetta: Rosetta is a widely used computational platform for macromolecular modeling, design, and analysis, integrating physics-based energy functions with knowledge-based statistical potentials42. For Rosetta-based thermostability optimization, we used the Rosetta ddG and Rosetta FastDesign protocols to perform sequence redesign aimed at improving folding stability. Specifically, starting from the experimentally determined or AlphaFold2-predicted protein structure, iterative rounds of side-chain repacking and backbone minimization were performed, guided by the Rosetta energy function. Each design trajectory generated multiple variants, and 1000 candidate sequences were obtained for each protein. The designed sequences were ranked according to Rosetta’s energy scores, with the top 100 lowest-energy conformations selected as putative thermostable variants.

Evaluating the Similarity to Natural Proteins

To evaluate the similarity of PGM-generated proteins to natural ones, we employed several methods. Firstly, we used MMseqs273 to determine the sequence identity between the generated proteins and natural proteins. Additionally, we predicted the structure of the generated proteins using AlphaFold23, ESMFold30 and USMFold, while assessed the structural identity to natural proteins using Foldseek74. The final structural identity of the generated proteins was determined by calculating the median structural identity among the structures predicted by the three methods. For each generated protein, we compared it to a collection of natural proteins obtained from the UniProt database29. The highest value obtained from these comparisons was considered as the final sequence and structure identity of the generated protein. This comprehensive evaluation allowed us to assess the similarity of the generated proteins to their natural counterparts accurately.

Gene Synthesis and Vector Construction

Gene encoding the protein that was to be validated was synthesized by Sino Biological (Beijing, China). To construct the expression clones, the synthesized gene and the destination vectors were digested using specific restriction enzymes (NdeI and XhoI, New England Biolabs, Cat# R0111 and R0146) according to the manufacturer's protocol. The digested fragments were purified and then ligated using T4 DNA Ligase (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# EL0011) at a molar ratio of 1:3 (vector to insert) for 2 hours at 25°C. The protein expression vector is pcDNA3.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# A14697) for eukaryotic HEK293 cells, pET-28a (Novagen, Cat# 69864) for prokaryotic E.coli cells, and pJL1 (Addgene, Plasmid #69496) for the cell-free expression system. To ensure the accuracy of the constructs, all vectors were verified by Sanger sequencing (Sino Biological, Beijing, China) using universal primers. Upon confirmation, high-purity plasmids were extracted and purified using the PureLink HQ 96 Plasmid DNA Purification Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# K210096) following the manufacturer's instructions.

Protein Expression in Eukaryotic HEK293 Cells

HEK293 cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# A14527) were cultured in FreeStyle 293 Expression Medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# 12338018). For small-scale screening, the recombinant pcDNA3.4 expression vectors were transfected into the cells seeded at a density of 1 × 10^6 cells/mL in a 24-well cell culture plate (700 μL per well). Transfection was performed using Linear Polyethylenimine (PEI, MW 25,000, Polysciences, Cat# 23966) with a DNA:PEI mass ratio of 1:3. Five days post-transfection, the culture supernatant was harvested by centrifugation at 1,000 × g for 10 minutes. For Western Blot analysis, samples were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto a PVDF membrane (Millipore, Cat# IPVH00010). After blocking with 5% non-fat milk in TBST for 1 hour, the membrane was incubated with His-Tag Antibody (HRP) (GenScript, Cat# A00612) at a 1:5,000 dilution for 1 hour at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using Pierce ECL Western Blotting Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# 32106) with a fixed exposure time. The relative expression levels were quantified based on band intensity using ImageJ software. The candidates with the highest expression levels were selected for scale-up in 6-well plates, with 3 mL of cells per well transfected under the same conditions. After 5 days of expression, the supernatant was collected and incubated with HisPur Ni-NTA Magnetic Beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# 88831) at 4°C for 2 hours with gentle agitation. The beads were washed three times with Wash Buffer (50 mM NaH PO , 300 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). The target proteins were then eluted using Elution Buffer (50 mM NaH PO , 300 mM NaCl, 250 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). The purity and molecular weight of the eluted proteins were verified by SDS-PAGE using 4-20% Mini-PROTEAN TGX Precast Gels (Bio-Rad, Cat# 4561096) and stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250 (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# B0149).

Protein Expression in Prokaryotic E.coli Cells

The pET-28a expression vectors were transformed into chemically competent E. coli BL21(DE3) cells (Invitrogen, Cat# C600003) via the heat-shock method. A single colony was inoculated into 5 mL of LB medium (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# L3147) containing 50 μg/mL Kanamycin and grown overnight at 37°C. The culture was then diluted 1:100 into 50 mL of fresh LB medium. When the culture reached an OD of 0.6–0.8, protein expression was induced by adding IPTG (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# I6758) to a final concentration of 0.5 mM, followed by overnight incubation at 18°C with shaking at 220 rpm. After induction, cells were harvested by centrifugation at 5,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C. The cell pellet was resuspended in Lysis Buffer (50 mM NaH PO , 300 mM NaCl, pH 7.4) and subjected to sonication on ice using a Branson Sonifier. The resulting lysate was clarified by centrifugation at 12,000 × g for 30 minutes at 4°C. The supernatant was then incubated with 125 μL of Ni-charged MagBeads (GenScript, Cat# L00295) for 1 hour at 4°C to selectively enrich the poly-His-tagged target protein. For purification, the beads were washed three times with a Wash Buffer (50 mM NaH PO , 300 mM NaCl, and 10 mM imidazole, pH 7.4). The target protein was eluted using an Elution Buffer (50 mM NaH PO , 300 mM NaCl, and 150 mM imidazole, pH 7.4). The expression level and purity of the eluted protein were determined using SDS-PAGE with 4-20% Mini-PROTEAN TGX Precast Gels (Bio-Rad, Cat# 4561096) and visualized via Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining.

Protein Expression in Cell-free Expression System

For cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS), the pJL1 expression vectors were added to the Cell-free Protein Expression Kit (Sino Biological, Cat# CFKIT01). The reaction was performed in a total volume of 100 μL in a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube. The mixture was incubated at 30°C for 3 hours on an orbital shaker at a constant speed of 800 rpm. Following incubation, the crude reaction mixture was centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 10 minutes at 4°C to remove insoluble debris and pellets. The CFPS supernatant was collected and the target His-tagged proteins were purified using HisPur Ni-NTA Magnetic Beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# 88831). Between purification steps, samples underwent buffer exchange into Phosphate-Buffered Saline (PBS, pH 7.4) using Amicon Ultra-0.5 Centrifugal Filter Units (3 kDa MWCO, Millipore, Cat# UFC5003) to remove imidazole or other salts. The final purified protein was concentrated and exchanged into a storage buffer (PBS with 10% glycerol). The purity and concentration of the samples at each stage, as well as the final product, were assessed by SDS-PAGE and UV absorbance at OD using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# ND-2000). Uncropped SDS–PAGE scans corresponding to Figures 3c–e are provided in the Source Data.

Lysozyme Enzyme Activity Assessment

After protein purification, a small amount of the purified protein is taken and diluted for the assessment of its enzymatic activity. The enzymatic activity is measured using a lysozyme assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat#E22013), with hen lysozyme (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#L4919) used as a positive control. The lysozyme activity assay is conducted using Micrococcus lysodeikticus cell walls that are labeled to the extent that their fluorescence is quenched. Lysozyme action can alleviate this quenching effect, resulting in a significant increase in fluorescence that is directly proportional to the lysozyme activity. To perform the assay, 50 µL of a working suspension containing 50 µg/mL of DQ lysozyme substrate is added to each well of a microplate containing the diluted proteins. The reaction mixtures are then incubated for at least 30 minutes at 37°C, while being protected from light. Fluorescence intensity was measured using a Varioskan LUX Multimode Microplate Reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# VLBL00D0) equipped with standard fluorescein filters (Excitation/Emission: 494/518 nm). Enzymatic activity is quantified in Units (U), which is defined as the amount of enzyme required to produce a change in the absorbance at 450 nm of 0.001 units per minute, using a suspension of Micrococcus lysodeikticus as the substrate.

The lysozyme antibacterial enzymatic activity is measured using the Nuclease Activity QC System (SinoBiological, Cat#NE001) by Sino Biological, Inc. Lysozyme digestion of bacteria leads to the release of bacterial nucleases. The measurement of nuclease activity in the supernatant allows for the evaluation of bacterial disruption, which is indicative of the lysozyme's antibacterial enzymatic activity. To perform the assay, Escherichia coli in the logarithmic growth phase is collected by centrifugation. The bacteria are then washed five times with PBS buffer until no nuclease activity is detectable in the supernatant. The bacteria are resuspended and diluted in a resuspension buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 150 mM NaCl). Next, 100 μL of the bacterial suspension, 40 μL of the enzyme to be tested, and 4 μL of the nuclease fluorescent substrate are mixed together. The mixture is incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes, followed by the addition of a termination solution to stop the reaction. The resulting fluorescence (Ex/Em: 480/520 nm) was measured to quantify nuclease activity, reflecting the degree of bacterial lysis.

Chitinase Enzyme Activity Assessment

For the evaluation of chitinase-like activity, a small portion of the purified protein was diluted in assay buffer (200 mM sodium phosphate, pH 8.0). The reaction was initiated by mixing 20 µL of the diluted protein with 80 µL of the substrate solution, containing a final concentration of 125 µM 4-Methylumbelliferyl-beta-D-$N,N',N''-triacetylchitotrioside [Mu-(GlcNAc)3] (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# M5639).The reaction mixtures were incubated in black 96-well microplates (Greiner Bio-One, Cat# 655076) at specified temperatures (e.g., 37°C or 85°C) for 3-6 hours in a humidified incubator to prevent evaporation. The fluorescence signal of the released product, 4-methylumbelliferone (4-MU), was measured using a Varioskan LUX Multimode Microplate Reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# VLBL00D0) at an excitation wavelength of 372 nm and an emission wavelength of 445 nm. To quantify the enzymatic activity, a standard curve of 4-methylumbelliferone (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# M1381) was prepared under identical buffer and temperature conditions. One unit of activity (Uc) was defined as the amount of enzyme required to release 1 nmol of 4-methylumbelliferone per minute under the assay conditions.

Naming Rules of ORI-engineered Proteins

Functional proteins that have been validated through wet lab assays are assigned names consisting of a prefix followed by a number. The prefix consists of two parts separated by a hyphen ("-"). The first part, "TX," represents Tencent and Unknown, respectively. The second part consists of abbreviations indicating the type of protein. "C" represents Chitinase, "L" represents Lysozyme, "S" represents thermostable proteins, "R" represents proteins refined by RLWF models, and "ME" represents proteins with multi-enzyme function. The number following the prefix is used to differentiate proteins within the same category.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

He et al present a new language-model based protein design method and validate it by designing lysozymes and
chitinases. The paper claims that ORI enables de novo design, but there is no evidence of that in any section. Additionally,
the claims of designing better than natural enzymes have not been rigorously demonstrated. For these reasons, I consider
the paper to be misleading. There are other, perhaps less serious, problems with this paper, but I will focus only on these
two as they make this paper unpublishable.
De novo design:
De novo design means designing "from scratch", without natural templates. This is not done in this paper. The designs are
entirely within the natural sequence families. See Fig1. The median, represented by a dashed line, is at 96% sequence
identity. This is not de novo, but in addition, it's a very timid design. The authors conclude from this that their model is
excellent in designing validated proteins, but all it shows is that the model has memorised wild-type sequences. They then
cut the designs at a threshold of 90%, but this too is not de novo. All their designs are >35% sequence identity to a natural
template that carries out the same reaction. There are other design methods that enable robust design within sequence
families, but they don't and can't claim that they are de novo design methods. The repeated claims on "novelty" and "de
novo" in this paper are simply unfounded.
Designing proteins that are improved relative to natural ones:
The authors report that the lysozyme designs exhibit a 100-fold improvement over hen egg white lysozyme (HEWL). This
sounds impressive, but T4 lysozyme (T4L) is sold by Sigma and advertised as possessing 200-fold improved activity relative
to HEWL. T4L is within the training set and their design may be based on T4L, but the authors don't compare their designs'
activities to it, only relative to the less efficient HEWL. This is, again, simply misleading.
The highlight of the paper is the design of a multifunctional lysozyme/chitinase, which they claim is "entirely novel function
that have never existed before". This sounds impressive, but lysozyme and chitinase exhibit highly related catalytic
mechanisms and similar folds, and natural lysozymes and chitinases exhibit cross reactivities, albeit weaker than their
native activities. So this multifunctionality is entirely not novel and in fact exists in natural families.
To close, I reiterate that the paper suffers from other problems, but the three I briefly remarked on are sufficient to preclude
publication.

### Reviewer 2

This is a very exciting and ambitious paper. The ORI system represents a creative integration of autoregressive language
models (PGM), pre-trained function predictors (USM), and a reinforcement learning loop with wet-lab feedback (RLWF), all
scaffolded around a structured ontology framework. The paper demonstrates the ability to generate proteins with useful
properties—enzyme activity, thermostability, and even multi-enzyme functionality—highlighted by experimental validation of
several sequences that outperform natural enzymes like lysozyme and chitinase. Overall, and the authors make a
compelling case for ORI as a full-stack generative biology system.
That said, to me, there are several areas where the manuscript falls short—particularly in mathematical clarity,
benchmarking, and contextualization with respect to recent generative modeling frameworks. I really think this paper could
benefit from significantly more rigorous comparisons to state-of-the-art models, as well as stronger justification for many of
the modeling decisions made. Below are five major concerns:
1. The mathematical formulation of the model is super vague and inconsistent throughout. The PGM model is described as a
decoder-only autoregressive Transformer (similar to LLaMA), but the training objective, tokenization schema, and prompt
structure are never clearly defined. On page 6 and Figure 1, we see prompts such as <Homo><Oxidoreductase>
<EC:1.1.1.181>..., but how these are tokenized, embedded, and used as prefix context is never precisely described. Is the
ontology token fed at the first position only? How long are the ontology sequences relative to the generated protein tokens?
Moreover, the RLWF formulation in Figure 3 and page 13 is highly condensed. The modified DPO loss used in training is
only given symbolically, and the preference dataset construction lacks clarity around sampling, control baselines, and
reward shaping. I’d strongly recommend the authors formally define the loss functions and generative process in each
phase, perhaps using equations in an appendix, as the current level of abstraction is insufficient for replication.
2. The comparisons to other generative protein models are incomplete and dated. There is no discussion of recent
generative models like DPLM, EvoDiff, DiMA, MeMDLM or AMP-Diffusion, all of which have shown strong performance in
different protein design tasks using diffusion models. Similarly, discrete flow matching models like Dirichlet Flow Matching,
Fisher Flow Matching, Gumbel Softmax Flow Matching are absent—yet these models enable guided, conditional generation
in a way directly comparable to ORI's ontology-conditioned decoding -- these should all be cited. The manuscript suggests
that reinforcement learning is the key innovation, but in reality, most modern generative biology frameworks rely on guided
discrete sampling rather than RL, due to the instability and sample inefficiency of reward-based learning in high-dimensional
sequence space. The authors should at minimum cite these models and explain what advantages, if any, RLWF provides
over guided discrete sampling. Otherwise, I cannot recommend acceptance if the authors don't acknowledge the state-of-
the-art in the field.
3. From my analysis, the experiments lack clear baselines against either modern PLMs or modality-specific generative
models. The only comparisons made are to ProteinMPNN, ESM2, and natural protein statistics? There is no head-to-head
against recent structure-free models like ProteinSGM, ProGen3, PepTune -- all of which can also be used to condition
generation on properties like stability, non-toxicity and other function. Further, for domain-specific baselines, tools like
UniPTM (for PTM prediction), PTM-Mamba, for PTM-aware embedding, and DPAC (for DNA-protein design) offer directly
comparable pipelines. The authors argue that ORI integrates sequence, structure, and function into a single prompt, but they
never show why this yields better results than methods that integrate these features more explicitly (via joint contrastive
training, or structure-conditioned diffusion). I suggest the authors benchmark ORI-generated sequences against outputs from
these domain-specific, particularly on shared tasks.
4. The experimental benchmarks are promising but not comprehensive. This is a big claim, and so the authors should
spend some time optimizing their work. Figures 2–5 show strong wet-lab validation on lysozyme and chitinase targets, but all
results are focused on enzymes with naturally high expression and well-behaved domains. Where are the harder targets?
All experiments are also single-round selections with no comparison to a baseline design tool (i.e., structure-based docking
or traditional motif grafting). Even for thermostability optimization (Figure 4), the authors never compare ORI-designed
proteins to sequences generated by ProteinMPNN or structure-based optimization with Rosetta. I’d recommend testing ORI
on harder problems, kike flexible loops, intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), or viral glycoproteins—and benchmarking
against sequence-only models or structure-aware diffusion tools.
5. The literature review focuses almost entirely on highly cited or media-prominent papers (AlphaFold, ProteinMPNN,
ProGen) while omitting many state-of-the-art systems that define the actual technical frontier in generative biology. The
authors cite ProGen1 but not ProGen3 (which introduces functional conditioning), nor ESM-C (contact-aware language
modeling), nor FusOn-pLM (isoform-aware fusion modeling). The omission of Rinalmo and EvoFlow-RNA from the RNA
section is particularly surprising given their state-of-the-art performance. If the claim is that ORI is a general-purpose,
scalable generative system, the authors need to show that it outperforms or meaningfully differs from these prior systems:
and that it wasn’t just trained on more data with better engineering.
In summary, I believe ORI is an exciting and impactful system, but the authors need to be more rigorous in how they
describe, benchmark, and situate it. Without tighter math, stronger comparisons, and more comprehensive experiments, it’s
hard for me to evaluate what’s truly novel versus what’s just larger and better resourced.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by Bing He et al. introduces ORI (Ontology Reinforcement Iteration), an AI platform for protein design. The
system takes as input feature requests from users that are interpreted by an agent generating candidates that are filtered and
validated with in-vitro assays. Results are then used to reinforce the generative process until it meets the user requirements.
The manuscript presents a series of three applications illustrating the functionalities and use cases of ORI.
Overall ORI is a valuable tool with promising performances. However, the current presentation has several shortcomings
that could prevent the readers to fully appreciate its potential.
1) The background and literature review in the introduction is incomplete. The idea of using reinforcement learning and
experimental assays as feedback for molecular design is not new (e.g., work of Baker’s group). A comprehensive review of
previous contributions is mandatory to contextualize this work.
2) My next concern follows the previous comment. It is not clear to me what is the main innovation of this work. It would be
important to clarify the contribution. Unless I misunderstood it, it feels more like a software contribution. The ORI platform is a
pipeline integrating multiple tools. Although, each individual component is not conceptually new, their integration in a unified
workflow has value. If such case, it would be eventually interesting to expand the discussion about the integration/use in
experimental labs.
3) Unless I missed it, the manuscript does not provide comparison or benchmark with other software and methods (it brings
us back to my first comment). As such, it is difficult to fully assess the technical advances of ORI. The examples provide in
the results section are interesting but do not replace a complete and rigorous validation of the platform. A large-scale (and
more quantitative) experiment (In contrast to a specific use cases) would also provide more confidence in the generalization
of ORI.
4) The analysis of the case studies presented in the paper could also be refined. Looking at the global sequence and
structure similarity is not sufficient. Further investigations of the designed proteins would help to validate the impact of the
output. For instance, it is not clear if the samples have highly similar active sites or if it could be found in the training data. It
would be important to show that similar result could not be obtained with a classical fragment assembly option, and could
also help to rule out any leak of information (I am assuming it is ok but the manuscript could expand the discussion).
5) In general, I would advise revising the style of writing. Currently, the text uses a lot of unnecessary superlatives that do not
bring anything to the scientific discussion. Some terms should also be more carefully chosen (e.g., in Figure 1, ORI does not
“understand” the needs, maybe “interpret” or another formulation would be preferable), and some statements be better
justified (e.g., on page 4, the authors say that “ORI can predict the optimal sequence and structure” but optimal is a strong
claim that should be proved).

multifunctional nature of the lysozyme/chitinase as "entirely novel," we now acknowledge that lysozymes and
chitinases share related catalytic mechanisms and structural folds, and exhibit cross-reactivity, though weaker than
their native activities. Our work, therefore, does not represent a completely unprecedented function, but rather a
rationally engineered enhancement of an existing, latent multifunctionality. However, it is important to note that our
dual-function enzyme outperforms single-function enzymes in each activity, unlike natural bifunctional enzymes,
which typically show a reduction in activity for one of their functions.
To illustrate this, we performed a comparative analysis of the enzyme activity of our dual-function protein TX-ME
against Hevamine A (HA, PDB: LLO), the naturally occurring dual-function protein reported to exhibit the highest
lysozyme and chitinase activities, as well as against monofunctional enzymes, including T4 lysozyme (T4L, PDB:
216L) and Glycoside Hydrolase Family 18 chitinase (GH18C, PDB: 1HKK). All proteins were expressed using a
cell-free system, and their respective enzyme activities were evaluated in the same wet lab assay to ensure consistency
and comparability. TX-ME exhibited significantly higher lysozyme activity than T4L (relative activity = 2.227), and
greater chitinase activity than GH18C (relative activity = 1.314). This improvement is a key distinguishing feature
of our design. In contrast, the natural dual-function enzyme HA showed substantially lower lysozyme activity
(relative activity = 0.246) compared to T4L, and much weaker chitinase activity (relative activity = 0.203) compared
to GH18C (Figure 5F).
We have updated the manuscript to show the new results, highlighting that our multifunctional enzyme represents an
enhancement within the natural enzyme families, rather than a completely novel function. We hope this revision
addresses your concerns and more accurately represents the novelty and significance of our work. Thank you again
for your valuable feedback.

Added Results
Part 1:
As previously mentioned, our work with ORI has demonstrated its capacity to design proteins with enhanced functions
and properties. Building on this success, we sought to explore ORI’s potential further by designing a multifunctional
enzyme capable of exhibiting both lysozyme (EC 3.2.1.17) and chitinase (EC 3.2.1.14) activities. Lysozyme, known
for its antimicrobial properties, is commonly used as a natural preservative in the food industry, while chitinase plays
a key role in the degradation of chitin, a major component of insect and crustacean exoskeletons. Interestingly, some
types of lysozyme and chitinase share similar catalytic mechanisms and structural folds, such as the TIM barrel
(alpha/beta barrel). However, natural lysozymes and chitinases exhibit only weak cross-reactivity, with each enzyme
functioning primarily within its own specific domain. Notably, proteins like Hevamine A (HA), which exhibit both
lysozyme and chitinase activities, show much weaker enzymatic functions than those with a single, dedicated activity.
Designing a multi-enzyme protein with both lysozyme and chitinase functionalities, and ensuring it performs better
than single-function counterparts, presents a significant challenge.
Part 2:
We conducted a comparative analysis of the enzyme activity of TX-ME against the dual-function enzyme Hevamine
A (HA) (PDB: LLO) and monofunctional enzymes, including T4 lysozyme (T4L) (PDB: 216L) and Glycoside
Hydrolase Family 18 chitinase (GH18C) (PDB: 1HKK). All proteins were expressed using a cell-free system, and
their respective enzyme activities were evaluated in the same wet lab assay to ensure consistency and comparability.
TX-ME exhibited significantly higher lysozyme activity than T4L (relative activity = 2.227), and greater chitinase
activity than GH18C (relative activity = 1.314). In contrast, the natural dual-function enzyme HA showed
substantially lower lysozyme activity (relative activity = 0.246) compared to T4L, and much weaker chitinase activity
(relative activity = 0.203) compared to GH18C (Figure 5 D and 5E). These results underscore the enhanced
functionality of TX-ME, which outperforms both the monofunctional enzymes and the natural dual-function enzyme
HA in terms of catalytic activity for both lysozyme and chitinase activities. The significantly higher enzyme activities
observed for TX-ME suggest that the multi-functional design of the protein not only retains but also enhances the
individual functionalities compared to their natural or engineered counterparts.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This is a very exciting and ambitious paper. The ORI system represents a creative integration of autoregressive
language models (PGM), pre-trained function predictors (USM), and a reinforcement learning loop with wet-lab
feedback (RLWF), all scaffolded around a structured ontology framework. The paper demonstrates the ability to
generate proteins with useful properties—enzyme activity, thermostability, and even multi-enzyme functionality—
highlighted by experimental validation of several sequences that outperform natural enzymes like lysozyme and
chitinase. Overall, and the authors make a compelling case for ORI as a full-stack generative biology system.
That said, to me, there are several areas where the manuscript falls short—particularly in mathematical clarity,
benchmarking, and contextualization with respect to recent generative modeling frameworks. I really think this paper
could benefit from significantly more rigorous comparisons to state-of-the-art models, as well as stronger justification
for many of the modeling decisions made. Below are five major concerns:

we have explicitly defined the tokenization schema, ontology-conditioned prompts, and their relation to the generated

including the modified DPO loss. Furthermore, we clarified the construction of the preference dataset, including
sampling strategy, control baselines, and reward shaping. These additions, together with an appendix containing full

Added Methods:
Tokenizer Construction
We constructed a byte-pair encoding (BPE)54 tokenizer tailored for protein design, with a vocabulary size of 49,152.
To support flexibility in encoding heterogeneous biological inputs, we reserved 200 token IDs as special tokens, which
can be dynamically replaced at runtime to represent ontology terms, annotations, or experimental constraints. The
reserved token set is drawn from a comprehensive replacement resource pool encompassing digits, Latin and Greek
alphabets, punctuation (! " # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . / : ; < = > ? @ [ \ ] ^ _ ` { | } ~), whitespace characters
(space \t \n \r \x0b \x0c), custom tokens (<CLS>, <PAD>, <MASK>, <EOD>, <:>), and additional domain-specific
symbols (£, ¥, «, », ±, ·). This design ensures broad coverage for encoding biological prompt phrases and precise
parsing of specialized terminology, such as protein functional annotations and enzyme classification numbers (e.g.,
EC:1.1.1.181).
During tokenization, each protein sequence was segmented into BPE subword tokens, optimized to capture both short
functional motifs (e.g., catalytic triads, signal peptides) and long repetitive patterns (e.g., coiled-coils, tandem
repeats). Ontology inputs—including functional annotations, EC numbers, structural constraints, and protein family
names—were tokenized separately using the special token pool and subsequently concatenated with the protein
tokens to form unified input sequences. In total, this process produced over 60 billion tokens from the integrated
protein sequence and annotation datasets, which were used to train the PGM model.
The Protein Design Agent (PDA)
The Protein Design Agent (PDA) serves as the orchestration layer that translates user requirements into ontology
prompts and function calls to the Protein Generation Model (PGM). In our protein design agent (PDA), we use a
module similar to Gorilla22 and Toolformer23, to convert users’ task requirements to function calls of our models.
Supervised Fine-tuning with LoRA: To achieve this goal, we perform low-rank parameter adaption (LoRA) 51 on
the open-sourced large language model Gemma2-2B52. The model is fine-tuned for 1 epoch with a single pass of all
data. The batch size is 32 and the learning rate is 1e-4. The rank for LoRA is 16.
To obtain the training data, we use GPT4 to generate input and output pairs for each function and characteristic by
providing GPT4 with the input requirements and functionality description of each function and characteristic. The
inputs are the user’s requirements and the outputs are the corresponding function and characteristic ontology prompts
and model function calls. We also provide high-quality examples generated by human experts as examples to GPT4
for the generation. Finally, we collected 5000 pairs of data generated by GPT4 and used GPT4 to score these
generated data based on the scope of requirements and the correctness of ontology prompts and function calls. We
further validated the correctness of the data with human experts. We used the top 2000 scoring data pairs for training.
In addition, to detect unsupported requirements, we extracted 200 input prompts from the Stanford Alpaca dataset
and designated the corresponding outputs as “unsupported”.

Overall Training Objective: The PDA training proceeded in two stages:
1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using cross-entropy loss to learn accurate mappings from user requirements to

The Protein Generation Model (PGM)
To train the protein generation model (PGM), we adopt a prompt-based encoding schema. The sequence begins with
ontology tokens that provide conditioning context, introduced at the first position of the sequence. The ontology
context typically contains 5–30 tokens, depending on the granularity of the annotation (e.g., “enzyme class
EC:1.1.1.181” or “IgG1 antibody heavy chain”). In contrast, protein sequences are substantially longer, ranging
from 100 to 1000 tokens after BPE segmentation. The input structure follows the format:
<CLS> Ontology_Tokens <:> Protein_Tokens <EOD>
This design ensures that ontology context acts as a prefix, guiding generation while preserving autoregressive protein
modeling. All tokens (protein and ontology) are mapped into a shared embedding space via a learnable embedding
layer. Positional encodings are applied to preserve order. Ontology tokens, although distinct in semantics, share the
embedding matrix with protein tokens to enable the transfer of contextual information. This joint representation
allows the PGM model to attend simultaneously to biological prompts and sequence context during self-attention,
enabling it to learn the statistical patterns and relationships among protein sequences, structures and biological
functions.
PGM is an autoregressive large language model that shares similarities with the decoder-only architecture used in
LLaMA serial models. PGM consists of embedding layers, multiple decoder blocks, and multilayer perceptron (MLP)
layers. The embedding layer maps each token to a continuous vector representation, capturing its unique properties.
The decoder blocks capture the sequential dependencies between tokens, allowing the model to learn the context and
relationships between functions and protein sequences. The decoder block follows the standard transformer
architecture55, applies RMSNorm for pre-normalization 56 and multi-head attentions, uses the SwiGLU activation
function 57, and rotary positional embeddings 58. The MLP layers consist of a fully connected layer and a
normalization layer, which are responsible for generating the final output tokens that represent the generated protein
sequences. The 3B PGM model consists of 24 decoder blocks and 24 multi-head attentions, with embedding
dimensions of 3072. For evaluation purposes, we also trained PGM models with parameter sizes of 1 billion (1B), 3
billion (3B) and 7 billion (7B). The annotated UniRef90 dataset and UniRef50 were utilized to train these models,
respectively. After evaluation, we used the 3B PGM model as the default protein generation model in ORI.
The model is trained under a causal language modeling (CLM) objective, predicting the next token given the

Iterative Optimization with Wet Lab Feedback
Wet lab experiments are crucial in developing protein generative models as they provide valuable biological insights
into the functionalities of the generated proteins. These insights are essential for validating the accuracy and
effectiveness of the models. However, it is often observed that only a subset of these proteins exhibit the desired
functionalities and activities, while the majority do not show significant activity. To improve the performance of these
models, researchers often analyze the outcomes of wet lab experiments and devise heuristic methods to refine or
retrain the models. However, this approach heavily relies on the subjective expertise of individual researchers, which
can introduce variability and limit reproducibility.
To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that is named Reinforcement Learning from Wet-lab
Feedback (RLWF). This framework utilizes feedback from wet lab experiments and selectively incorporates generated
data to optimize model preference. Doing so systematically increases the likelihood of generating protein sequences
with the targeted properties. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has been effectively employed
to optimize the output of Large Language Models (LLMs), aligning the generated responses with user preferences61.

Comment 2
2. The comparisons to other generative protein models are incomplete and dated. There is no discussion of recent
generative models like DPLM, EvoDiff, DiMA, MeMDLM or AMP-Diffusion, all of which have shown strong
performance in different protein design tasks using diffusion models. Similarly, discrete flow matching models like
Dirichlet Flow Matching, Fisher Flow Matching, Gumbel Softmax Flow Matching are absent—yet these models
enable guided, conditional generation in a way directly comparable to ORI's ontology-conditioned decoding -- these
should all be cited. The manuscript suggests that reinforcement learning is the key innovation, but in reality, most
modern generative biology frameworks rely on guided discrete sampling rather than RL, due to the instability and
sample inefficiency of reward-based learning in high-dimensional sequence space. The authors should at minimum
cite these models and explain what advantages, if any, RLWF provides over guided discrete sampling. Otherwise, I
cannot recommend acceptance if the authors don't acknowledge the state-of-the-art in the field.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and fully agree that our initial version did not
sufficiently acknowledge recent state-of-the-art generative frameworks. In the revised manuscript, we have
substantially expanded the Introduction to include relevant diffusion-based protein generation models such as DPLM,
EvoDiff, DiMA, MeMDLM, and AMP-Diffusion, as well as discrete flow matching models including Dirichlet Flow
Matching, Fisher Flow Matching, and Gumbel Softmax Flow Matching. These works are now appropriately cited
and discussed.
To avoid confusion, we explicitly acknowledge that ORI’s ontology-conditioned decoding constitutes a form of
guided discrete sampling, comparable in spirit to these diffusion and flow-matching frameworks. We have revised
the text to reflect this conceptual alignment.
At the same time, we emphasize that ORI goes beyond guided sampling by incorporating reinforcement learning
with experimental feedback (RLWF). As the reviewer correctly notes, guided discrete sampling is often more stable
and sample-efficient in high-dimensional sequence space. However, RLWF offers complementary advantages: (i) it
allows optimization of non-differentiable or sparse functional objectives (e.g., thermostability, expression yield, wet-
lab activity assays) that cannot be directly incorporated into score-matching or flow-based objectives; and (ii) it
enables iterative improvement of the generative model by directly integrating experimental feedback loops, which is
essential for practical deployment in protein engineering pipelines. We believe this complementary role of RLWF
provides ORI with additional robustness and adaptability beyond existing guided sampling frameworks.
Added Introduction:
Part1:
Building on these foundations, cutting-edge generative approaches now span multiple technical paradigms. Methods
such as DPLM10and EvoDiff11 apply diffusion directly in sequence space to capture evolutionary constraints, while
DiMA12 and MeMDLM13 leverage latent or discrete diffusion to improve controllability and enable applications like
membrane protein design. ProteinSGM14 extends score-based generative modeling to protein sequences, offering
another powerful diffusion paradigm.
Part2:
Specialized frameworks like PepTune16 and AMP-Diffusion17 further highlight the potential of generative models in
therapeutic peptide design, optimizing multiple objectives and targeting antimicrobial activity.
Part3:
Parallel to these, discrete flow matching frameworks—including Dirichlet Flow Matching, Fisher Flow Matching,
and Gumbel Softmax Flow Matching—have emerged as promising alternatives, enabling guided and conditional
generation in discrete sequence spaces20. Together, these approaches exemplify the prevailing paradigm of guided
discrete sampling in modern generative biology.
Part4:
Building on these insights, we introduce ORI (Ontology Reinforcement Iteration), a general-purpose and scalable
framework for generating functional proteins. ORI unifies ontology-conditioned decoding with reinforcement
learning with experimental feedback (RLWF) into a single system. Its innovations include: (1) using structured
ontologies as semantic prompts to inject functional, structural, and property-level constraints into the generative
process, enabling controllable and interpretable sequence generation; (2) combining the controllability of guided
discrete sampling with the ability of RL to directly optimize sparse or non-differentiable objectives; and (3)
implementing a closed-loop evolutionary cycle that involves generation, experimental measurement, feedback-driven
reward assignment, ontology refinement, and model updating, thereby enabling the co-evolution of both the
generative model and its ontology. In this way, ORI leverages the strengths of guided sampling and RL simultaneously,
addressing limitations of prior methods and enabling robust, multi-objective protein engineering in real-world
settings.
Comment 3
3. From my analysis, the experiments lack clear baselines against either modern PLMs or modality-specific
generative models. The only comparisons made are to ProteinMPNN, ESM2, and natural protein statistics? There is
no head-to-head against recent structure-free models like ProteinSGM, ProGen3, PepTune -- all of which can also be
used to condition generation on properties like stability, non-toxicity and other function. Further, for domain-specific
baselines, tools like UniPTM (for PTM prediction), PTM-Mamba, for PTM-aware embedding, and DPAC (for DNA-
protein design) offer directly comparable pipelines. The authors argue that ORI integrates sequence, structure, and
function into a single prompt, but they never show why this yields better results than methods that integrate these
features more explicitly (via joint contrastive training, or structure-conditioned diffusion). I suggest the authors
benchmark ORI-generated sequences against outputs from these domain-specific, particularly on shared tasks.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment regarding baselines. Following the suggestion, we
have expanded our comparisons to include ProteinSGM, ProGen3, and EVO2, representing recent advances in
structure-based, sequence-based, and DNA-based generative models, respectively. We benchmarked these models
alongside ORI on the central task of conditioned protein generation, assessing the generated proteins using structural
confidence, functional relevance metrics, and thermostability. The results are now presented in Supplementary
Figures 2, 3, and 6. These additional baselines provide a more complete and transparent context for evaluating ORI’
s performance relative to modern state-of-the-art methods.
For other models mentioned by the reviewer, including PepTune, UniPTM, PTM-Mamba, and DPAC, our current
framework does not directly overlap with their task definitions or model scope. Therefore, we were unable to perform
head-to-head benchmarking against these methods. We fully agree, however, that these systems represent important
points of comparison. To address this, we have added a discussion of these domain-specific generative systems and
explicitly acknowledged the limitations of our current evaluation, noting that future extensions of ORI should include
benchmarking on PTM-aware and DNA–binding-protein design tasks.
We hope these revisions improve the fairness and completeness of the evaluation, while transparently discussing the
current limitations of our model.

Added Methods
Benchmark with Baseline Methods
To comprehensively evaluate ORI, we benchmarked it against a wide range of recent state-of-the-art models,
spanning conditioned protein generation and thermostability optimization.
ProteinSGM: ProteinSGM is a score-based diffusion model that produces native-like protein structures14. We used
the crystal structure of hen egg-white lysozyme (PDB ID: 132L) and T4 lysozyme (PDB ID: 216L) as a template,
where specific regions were masked to provide partial structural information as input. ProteinSGM was then used to
generate 1000 conditional 6D coordinates from the ProteinSGM model, including Cβ–Cβ distances, ω and θ dihedral
angles, and ϕ planar angles. These coarse-grained 6D representations were then converted into full-atom protein
backbones using Rosetta MinMover46, which performed constrained backbone minimization to ensure physically
realistic geometries.
ProGen3: ProGen3 is an autoregressive protein language model designed for sequence generation15. We provided
the sequences of hen egg-white lysozyme (PDB ID: 132L) and T4 lysozyme (PDB ID: 216L) as conditioning contexts.
Using these templates, we employed the ProGen3-3B model to generate amino acid sequences in both N-to-C
(forward) and C-to-N (reverse) directions, conditioned on the functional and sequence constraints. A total of 1000
protein sequences were sampled, ensuring coverage of diverse sequence space.
Evo2: Evo 2 is a large-scale biological foundation model trained on 9.3 trillion DNA bases that learns genome-wide
biological features directly from DNA sequence, enabling accurate prediction of functional variants and controllable
genome-scale sequence generation41. For Evo2-based conditional protein generation, we first designed functional
prompts according to the model’s requirements, encoding structural and biochemical features of target proteins.
Specifically, we constructed text-based prompts describing hen egg-white lysozyme (PDB ID: 132L) and T4 lysozyme
(PDB ID: 216L), including their structural class, enzymatic activity, and functional attributes. Conditioned on these
prompts, Evo2 was used to generate 1,000 DNA sequences for each protein, ensuring that the outputs satisfied the
specified biochemical and functional constraints. The generated DNA sequences were subsequently translated into
protein sequences, followed by filtering to remove incomplete or invalid coding regions before downstream evaluation.
ProteinMPNN: ProteinMPNN is a graph-based generative model for protein sequence design conditioned on
backbone structures43. For thermostability optimization, we first predicted the backbone structure of each target
protein using AlphaFold26, which served as the input scaffold. ProteinMPNN was then applied to redesign the amino
acid sequences on this backbone. For each target, we generated 1000 redesigned variants and selected the top 100
candidates based on the predicted stability score. The redesigned sequences were further filtered by predicted folding
quality (pLDDT > 70) to ensure structural plausibility.
Rosetta: Rosetta is a widely used computational platform for macromolecular modeling, design, and analysis,
integrating physics-based energy functions with knowledge-based statistical potentials46. For Rosetta-based
thermostability optimization, we used the Rosetta ddG and Rosetta FastDesign protocols to perform sequence
redesign aimed at improving folding stability. Specifically, starting from the experimentally determined or
AlphaFold2-predicted protein structure, iterative rounds of side-chain repacking and backbone minimization were
performed, guided by the Rosetta energy function. Each design trajectory generated multiple variants, and 1000
candidate sequences were obtained for each protein. The designed sequences were ranked according to Rosetta’s
energy scores, with the top 100 lowest-energy conformations selected as putative thermostable variants.
Added Discussion:
While ORI demonstrates strong performance across diverse protein design tasks, we recognize important limitations
in its current scope. Domain-specific generative systems such as PepTune18 for peptide generation and optimization,
UniPTM51 and PTM-Mamba52 for post-translational modification (PTM)–aware modeling, and DPAC53 for DNA–
binding-protein prediction and design adopt specialized architectures and training objectives that explicitly integrate
functional constraints not yet captured by ORI. In addition, many challenging protein classes remain outside the
present design space. Proteins with highly flexible loops or intrinsically disordered regions, such as therapeutic
peptides and antibodies, pose unique challenges due to their conformational heterogeneity and context-dependent
activity. Proteins with extensive post-translational modifications, including viral glycoproteins decorated with glycan
shields, further complicate design because of their dynamic structures and roles in immune evasion. Moving forward,
extending ORI to handle these more complex protein classes and systematically benchmarking it against specialized
domain-specific models will be a critical direction for development.

Added Introduction:
Building on these foundations, cutting-edge generative approaches now span multiple technical paradigms. Methods
such as DPLM10and EvoDiff11 apply diffusion directly in sequence space to capture evolutionary constraints, while
DiMA12 and MeMDLM13 leverage latent or discrete diffusion to improve controllability and enable applications like
membrane protein design. ProteinSGM14 extends score-based generative modeling to protein sequences, offering
another powerful diffusion paradigm. In parallel, large-scale language models such as ProGen315 demonstrate the
benefits of scaling for controllable and high-quality protein generation. ESM-C extended language modeling to
explicitly incorporate structural contact information16, while FusOn-pLM enabled isoform-aware fusion modeling17.
These developments broaden the applicability of protein language models for functional protein engineering.
Specialized frameworks like PepTune18 and AMP-Diffusion19 further highlight the potential of generative models in
therapeutic peptide design, optimizing multiple objectives and targeting antimicrobial activity. Parallel to these,
discrete flow matching frameworks—including Dirichlet Flow Matching, Fisher Flow Matching, and Gumbel
Softmax Flow Matching—have emerged as promising alternatives, enabling guided and conditional generation in
discrete sequence spaces20. Together, these approaches exemplify the prevailing paradigm of guided discrete
sampling in modern generative biology.
Beyond proteins, advances have also been made in RNA generative modeling. Systems such as Rinalmo21 and
EvoFlow-RNA22 achieve state-of-the-art performance in RNA sequence design and structure prediction,
demonstrating the feasibility of applying generative frameworks to biomolecules beyond proteins. Collectively, these
developments indicate a clear trend: generative models are moving from merely capturing sequence–structure
relationships toward integrating optimization signals into the generation process, directly guiding functional
improvements.
Despite rapid methodological advances, key challenges remain in functional protein design. Many existing models
perform well when structural priors are available—such as in the design of regular folds or ligand-binding motifs—
but struggle when only subtle functional differences exist among highly similar structures, or when designing novel
functions without appropriate templates. In such cases, structural priors may be incomplete or even misleading,
reducing design efficiency and accuracy. Moreover, the mapping from sequence variation to folding, stability, and
function is highly complex, leading to high experimental failure rates and resource-intensive trial-and-error
workflows.
To address these challenges, researchers have explored different strategies for integrating functional optimization
signals into generative models. Guided sampling approaches, including diffusion and flow matching, offer stability
and sample efficiency when the objective is differentiable or can be approximated. However, these methods are limited
when the target objective is sparse, noisy, or non-differentiable—such as enzyme activity, expression levels,
thermostability, or other experimental phenotypes. Reinforcement learning (RL) combined with experimental assays
has emerged as an alternative: pioneering studies from Baker’s group and others have shown the feasibility of
iterative design guided by experimental feedback, and follow-up frameworks (e.g., EVOLVEpro) have adopted
similar principles in active learning or small-sample settings23,24. While RL is attractive for directly optimizing non-
differentiable objectives, existing approaches often face issues of instability and low sample efficiency in the high-
dimensional sequence space, and most prior implementations remain constrained to specific scaffolds or narrowly
defined targets.

We further analyzed the ORI-designed proteins that successfully exhibited dual-enzyme activities by comparing them

Added Discussion

novo through a generative language model that captures continuous representations of the sequence–structure–
function landscape. Rather than recombining known sequence or structural fragments, ORI learns the statistical
dependencies between amino acid sequences, protein structures, and functional annotations within a unified latent
space. During generation, ontology-conditioned decoding guides the model to produce sequences that satisfy specific
functional constraints while maintaining structural plausibility. This mechanism enables ORI to explore novel
